analysis.one_liner: Pays CFPB whistleblowers 10–30% of sanctions their tips help collect.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 8 Senate Democrats, got a Senate Banking Committee hearing in July 2020 but never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to pay cash rewards to insiders who report consumer financial law violations — like predatory lending or debt collection abuse — when the bureau's enforcement action brings in more than $1 million in sanctions. Whistleblowers would get 10% to 30% of what the bureau actually collects, paid out of the bureau's civil penalty fund rather than taxpayer money. The bill also guarantees confidentiality for whistleblowers and bars companies from using pre-dispute arbitration clauses to block these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, who gain a stronger enforcement pipeline: the people who witness wrongdoing inside banks, payday lenders, debt collectors, and other financial firms get a real financial reason to come forward, and the bureau gets a way to catch violations it could not see on its own. Whistleblowers themselves benefit from guaranteed anonymity protections, legal representation requirements, and protection from being forced into arbitration by their employers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CFPB to pay whistleblowers 10%–30% of collected monetary sanctions when their original information leads to an enforcement action exceeding $1 million, mirroring the incentive structure of the SEC's whistleblower program
Provides a floor award of $50,000 (or 10% of what is collected, whichever is greater) even when the bureau cannot collect the full $1 million in sanctions
Bars the bureau and its employees from disclosing information that could reveal a whistleblower's identity, and allows anonymous claims through counsel
Makes pre-dispute arbitration agreements unenforceable for disputes under the program and bars employers from using employment agreements to waive these rights
Awards are paid from the Consumer Financial Civil Penalty Fund — money collected from violators — rather than from general taxpayer revenue

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms that violate consumer financial laws: they face a greater risk that employees will report them to the CFPB, and penalties, disgorgement, and restitution collected from violators would fund the whistleblower awards. Employers of whistleblowers also lose the ability to force these disputes into private arbitration.
analysis.who_pays_short: Financial firms that break consumer laws

drawbacks.text: Cash-for-tips programs can generate a flood of low-quality or duplicative reports; the bill guards against this with an 'original information' requirement and denials for repeat or bad-faith claims, but the bureau would bear the cost of screening the additional volume

The bill strips defendants of virtually all ability to appeal award decisions — a court may review only whether the bureau could make an award at all, not whether the amount was reasonable, and even then only within 30 days
The $50,000 minimum award in small cases, drawn from the penalty fund, could drain money that would otherwise flow to victims of the underlying violations

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is favorable to the public: the program is self-funding out of penalties imposed on violators, and the main cost is administrative burden and some award-award disputes at the bureau. The screening rules in the bill — original-information requirements, denial for bad actors, and prosecution for false statements — address the most obvious failure modes of a cash-for-tips program. The near-total elimination of appeals for whistleblowers whose awards were made is a real due-process rough edge for companies, though courts would still review whether an award could be made at all.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee held a hearing on the bill in July 2020 but never voted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on June 17, 2020, joined by seven Democratic cosponsors including Sens. Brown, Warren, Smith, Durbin, Merkley, Wyden, and Blumenthal
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
The committee held a hearing on the bill on July 29, 2020 (printed as S.Hrg. 116-441), the only action beyond introduction
No further action — no committee vote, no floor vote — occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021
All seven cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on
A nearly identical structure already exists at the Securities and Exchange Commission, whose whistleblower program has paid substantial awards for tips leading to enforcement

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms that might have been reported to the CFPB by insiders are better off: without the reward program, there was one less financial incentive for employees to come forward, and the bureau lost a low-cost enforcement tool. No one else bore a cost from the bill dying.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms that escaped insider tips

sides.party_line_note: All 8 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Senate Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never took the bill beyond a hearing.

industries.industry: Banks and consumer financial firms (payday lenders, debt collectors, mortgage servicers)
industries.note: The bill raises the odds that internal wrongdoing reaches the CFPB by giving employees a 10–30% share of sanctions, and their penalty payments would fund the awards. Their interest in avoiding enforcement runs directly against consumers' interest in it.

The bill makes pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for whistleblower reward claims, removing a tool employers use to keep these disputes out of court. The public keeps the right to have such disputes heard rather than forced into private arbitration.
